# Hermes Agent + k3s + NVIDIA OpenShell — Self-Hosting and LLM Billing

Full analysis. Every factual claim carries an inline `[N]` to
[citations.md](citations.md). Two independent audit agents
([citation-audit](audit/citation-audit.md),
[consistency-review](audit/consistency-review.md)) verified this document against the
cited sources.

## Question

Evaluate self-hosting **Hermes Agent** (`hermes-agent.nousresearch.com`, Nous Research)
alongside a **k3s** cluster and **NVIDIA OpenShell** for sandboxed agent execution, with
emphasis on how the agent consumes LLMs and whether a **Claude Code / Claude
subscription** can back it or whether it is **API pay-per-token only**.

## TL;DR

1. **Hermes Agent** is an MIT-licensed, provider-agnostic autonomous agent that lives on
   your server, with persistent memory, a learning loop, and an OpenAI-compatible API
   server [1][4][5]. It brings the agent; it does not bring the model [3][5].
2. **NVIDIA OpenShell** (Apache 2.0) is a policy-governed sandbox runtime; **NemoClaw**
   (Apache 2.0) is NVIDIA's reference stack that explicitly runs "agents like **Hermes**"
   inside OpenShell [7][10]. This is the supported integration glue — Hermes' own docs
   never mention OpenShell [5][6].
3. **k3s fit:** OpenShell's `kubernetes` compute driver provisions sandboxes via the
   Kubernetes SIG `agent-sandbox` project and deploys its gateway by Helm from GHCR
   [8][9]. k3s is **not named** by NVIDIA but, as conformant Kubernetes, is
   *expected-to-work-but-unverified* [8]; the chart is **experimental, "do not use in
   production"** [9].
4. **Billing (the crux):** a Claude **Pro/Max subscription cannot legitimately back**
   Hermes — Anthropic blocked subscription OAuth in third-party agentic tools (policy
   Feb 20, 2026; technical block Apr 4, 2026) [15][16]. The compliant Claude path is an
   **API key (pay-per-token)** [12][13], a cloud provider [2], or **Nous Portal** (a
   *different* subscription you pay Nous for) [3]. Self-hosting a local model takes LLM
   cost to zero [2][6].

## 1. What Hermes Agent is

Hermes Agent is Nous Research's autonomous agent: "an autonomous agent that lives on your
server, remembers what it learns, and gets more capable the longer it runs" [1]. It is
**MIT-licensed and free** [5][6], installs by a single `curl … install.sh` command [5],
and ships 40+ tools (terminal, file ops, web search, memory, skills) [4][5]. Its
signature feature is a learning loop that auto-generates skills and persists multi-level
memory across sessions [1]. It connects to many frontends (Telegram, Discord, Slack, CLI,
etc.) [1][5] and runs anywhere from "a $5 VPS [to] a GPU cluster [to] serverless" [5].

Crucially for this evaluation, Hermes exposes an **OpenAI-compatible API server** at
`POST /v1/chat/completions` (plus `/v1/responses`, Runs/Jobs/Sessions APIs) and runs its
full toolset server-side [4]. Detail: [hermes-agent-overview.md](references/hermes-agent-overview.md).

## 2. How the agent consumes an LLM

Hermes is a **harness, not a model** [3][5]. It calls any chat model through a provider
abstraction and you "switch models without code changes" [5]. Nous's own Hermes 4
(70B/405B) exists but is **not recommended** for the tool-calling loop; the docs point to
frontier agentic models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Pro) [3]. Providers span
direct cloud APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini), routers (OpenRouter, LiteLLM), the Nous
Portal gateway, enterprise cloud (Bedrock, Azure), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible
backends (vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, Ollama) [2]. Self-hosted backends need tool-calling
enabled (e.g. vLLM `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser hermes`) [2].

The consequence: **Hermes adds no LLM markup — the cost model is the provider's** [6]. The
"can I use a Claude subscription" question is therefore purely about the Anthropic provider
path. Detail: [agent-llm-consumption.md](references/agent-llm-consumption.md).

## 3. Sandboxing: Hermes' own vs OpenShell on k3s

Hermes has *built-in* sandboxing — "Real Sandboxing" across five backends (local, Docker,
SSH, Singularity, Modal) with container hardening and namespace isolation [1]. This is
process/container-level, not kernel-policy, and not Kubernetes-native.

**NVIDIA OpenShell** (Apache 2.0) is the stronger, external runtime: "the safe, private
runtime for autonomous AI agents," governed by declarative YAML policies across four
domains — filesystem, network, process, and **inference** [7]. The gateway is the auth
boundary; every outbound connection is intercepted and allowed, **routed for inference
with credential injection**, or denied [7]. (Kernel mechanism — Landlock LSM, seccomp BPF,
OPA/Rego proxy — is documented in the prior
[openshell-security-boundary](../openshell-security-boundary/) research.)

**NemoClaw** (Apache 2.0) is the bridge: "a reference stack for running always-on AI agents
more safely inside NVIDIA OpenShell sandboxes," naming "agents like **Hermes** and
OpenClaw," with routed inference, network policy, and a lifecycle CLI [10].

**k3s path:** OpenShell drivers are `docker`/`podman`/`kubernetes`/`vm` [8]. The
`kubernetes` driver provisions `agents.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1` Sandbox resources via the
Kubernetes SIG `agent-sandbox` project, supports GPU scheduling, and deploys its gateway by
Helm (`oci://ghcr.io/nvidia/openshell/helm-chart`) as a StatefulSet — after you install the
Agent Sandbox controller + CRDs [8][9]. **k3s is not named by NVIDIA**; applicability is a
flagged inference (conformant Kubernetes) [8]. The chart is **experimental — "Do not use it
in production"** [9].

Reference topology:

```
k3s cluster
 ├─ Agent Sandbox controller + CRDs        (prereq) [9]
 ├─ OpenShell gateway (Helm StatefulSet)    auth boundary + policy engine [7][9]
 │    └─ inference policy: inject LLM credential, route egress [7]
 └─ Sandbox pod (agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox)   [8]
      └─ Hermes Agent (via NemoClaw blueprint) [10]
           ├─ OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions → your frontends [4]
           └─ LLM calls → (OpenShell-routed) Anthropic API key │ Nous Portal │ local vLLM
```

The **inference** policy domain is what ties sandboxing to billing: OpenShell can hold the
LLM credential and inject it at the proxy, so the sandboxed Hermes process never sees the
raw key and cannot exfiltrate it or call unapproved endpoints [7]. Detail:
[k3s-openshell-sandboxing.md](references/k3s-openshell-sandboxing.md).

## 4. Billing: subscription vs API

**Short answer: Claude API key (pay-per-token), not a Claude Pro/Max subscription.**

Hermes' provider doc lists a Claude subscription-reuse path — "OAuth (requires Claude
Max + extra usage credits)" and "Claude Code credential reuse" (`--provider claude-code`)
[2] — but that conflicts with current Anthropic policy:

- Anthropic **prohibits subscription OAuth in third-party tools**: Free/Pro/Max tokens
  "cannot be used outside Claude Code and Claude.ai"; use an API key instead [15].
  Effective **Feb 20, 2026** (policy) [15], with a **technical block from Apr 4, 2026** for
  "all third-party agentic tools" (OpenClaw, OpenCode named) [16]. Hermes is such a tool.
- Anthropic's support doc grants subscription coverage only to its own surfaces + supported
  IDEs, and notes that setting `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` yields **API charges**, not subscription
  usage [12].
- Internal corroboration: OAuth tokens are rejected at `/v1/messages`; Agent-SDK auth is
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` ([claude-code-oauth-quota](../claude-code-oauth-quota/)).

So the `claude-code` reuse line in Hermes' docs [2] is **stale or ToS-violating** for
Pro/Max post-April-2026. Compliant Claude options: **Anthropic API key**, **Bedrock/Vertex**,
or **Nous Portal**.

**The subscription that does work is Nous Portal** — one OAuth login, one credit balance,
300+ models including Claude [3]. You pay Nous, not via your Anthropic subscription;
per-token/credit rate is unpublished on the fetched page [3].

**Cost reality.** Hermes is free; you pay only LLM usage [6]. Current Anthropic base rates
[13]: Opus 4.8/4.7/4.6 $5/$25 per MTok (in/out); Sonnet 4.6 $3/$15; Haiku 4.5 $1/$5;
deprecated Opus 4/4.1 $15/$75. Pro $20/mo, Max from $100/mo [14].

> **Contradiction surfaced.** A widely-cited figure [16] pegs a heavy Opus-4.6 agent (500K
> in + 200K out tokens/day) at **~$675/mo (≈3.4× a $200 Max plan)** — but it used the
> **deprecated $15/$75** Opus rate, not current Opus 4.6 **$5/$25** [13]. Recomputed:
> `(0.5×$5)+(0.2×$25) = $7.50/day ≈ $225/mo (est.)` — roughly at par with Max, not 3.4×
> over. The Opus 4.7+ tokenizer (up to +35% tokens) [13] pushes it to **~$255–305/mo
> (est.)**; Sonnet 4.6 for the same volume is **~$135/mo (est.)**. The directional point
> (no subscription discount ⇒ higher cost) holds; the magnitude in [16] is ~3× overstated
> for current models.

Detail and full decision table: [billing-subscription-vs-api.md](references/billing-subscription-vs-api.md).

## 5. Self-hosting feasibility verdict

| Factor | Assessment |
|--------|-----------|
| Agent licensing | Green — MIT, free, single-command install [5][6] |
| Hermes ↔ OpenShell integration | Green — first-class via NemoClaw [10] |
| k3s deployment | **Amber** — `kubernetes` driver exists [8] but k3s unnamed; gateway chart **experimental, not for production** [9]; needs Agent Sandbox CRDs [9] |
| LLM via Claude subscription | **Red** — blocked by Anthropic since Apr 2026 [15][16] |
| LLM via Claude API key / Bedrock | Green — compliant, pay-per-token [2][12][13] |
| LLM via Nous Portal | Green — works; pricing opaque [3] |
| LLM via self-hosted model | Green — zero per-token cost, needs GPU [2][6][8] |

**Bottom line.** The stack is coherent and NVIDIA-blessed (Hermes-in-OpenShell via
NemoClaw), and k3s is a plausible host through the Kubernetes driver — but the K8s path is
explicitly pre-production [9], and you should plan for an **Anthropic API key, a cloud
provider, Nous Portal, or a self-hosted model** rather than a Claude Pro/Max subscription
[15][16]. If avoiding per-token LLM spend is the goal, the GPU-scheduling-capable k3s
cluster [8] is exactly the place to host a local tool-calling model and point Hermes at it
[2][6].

## Limitations

- k3s never named by NVIDIA; applicability is inference [8].
- Ban effective-date conflict (Feb 20 vs Apr 4) across two secondary sources; Anthropic's
  underlying policy not fetched as a standalone primary [15][16].
- Nous Portal and NemoClaw routed-inference pricing/model unpublished [3][10].
- Cost figures past the cited rate tables are illustrative **(est.)**, not measured Hermes
  traces.
- Multi-engine (DuckDuckGo) search augmentation was not run; coverage rests on WebSearch +
  direct vendor/primary fetches.
